articles.title: The Notebook Is the Tool
articles.excerpt: For a while I thought the useful part of testing a phone was the moment of judgment: after an hour of play, you decide whether it was good or bad. I now think that judgment is the least useful artifac…
articles.body: For a while I thought the useful part of testing a phone was the moment of judgment: after an hour of play, you decide whether it was good or bad. I now think that judgment is the least useful artifact in the whole process, because it compresses an hour into a sentence and throws away every minute that made the hour what it was. What I do instead is embarrassingly simple. A small notebook, two columns: the time, and one line about what changed. Every fifteen minutes I write one line. No scores, no adjectives if I can help it. "11:15 - back panel noticeably warm, framerate still fine." That is the whole method. After a few weeks of this the lines start to argue with your memory. Devices I remembered as stable for an hour turn out to have been degrading from minute twenty.
articles.author: Eka Putri

articles.title: Fixing Gitea Actions on Synology Container Manager
articles.excerpt: Gitea worked on my Synology NAS. Its CI jobs failed before they could check out a single file. I was hosting Gitea and its Actions runner through Synology Container Manager's Docker Compose support. T…
articles.body: Gitea worked on my Synology NAS. Its CI jobs failed before they could check out a single file. I was hosting Gitea and its Actions runner through Synology Container Manager's Docker Compose support . The server was running, but the runner could not create the container that would execute the workflow. None of the repository's code had run yet. The fix was to stop running a second Docker daemon inside the runner and use Synology's existing daemon instead. That removed the failing nested mount. It also gave CI access to the same daemon managing the other containers on my NAS. Those are two consequences of the same change. The Original Compose Configuration This was the starting configuration.

articles.title: Memory Séance Lite: A Private, Local AI Ofrenda for the Stories We Almost Forget
articles.excerpt: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine Every family has a ghost like this: a grandmother who named every tomato plant in her garden, an uncle'…
articles.body: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine What I Built Every family has a ghost like this: a grandmother who named every tomato plant in her garden, an uncle's terrible jokes, a side project that stopped at version 0.3 and has been rotting in a private repo ever since. They are not dramatic stories. They are small, specific, and they disappear the moment the last person who remembers them stops talking. Memory Séance Lite is a small app for keeping those stories. You write short memories about a person, a pet, a place, or an abandoned software project. They are saved in a SQLite file on your own computer. Then a small open-weight language model, running locally through Ollama, does two things: Writes an ofrenda.

articles.title: I fixed my homepage to name a person. Then I checked the page every article sends people to.
articles.excerpt: Last night I wrote about a reader who asked, bluntly, who is this app for? I searched the readable text of my own homepage and the words parent, student, nurse, shift worker, freelancer, teacher, chil…
articles.body: Last night I wrote about a reader who asked, bluntly, who is this app for? I searched the readable text of my own homepage and the words parent, student, nurse, shift worker, freelancer, teacher, child appeared zero times. Twenty-two thousand characters about habits, and not one person holding one. I fixed the homepage that night. A single paragraph in the hero now names her: the nurse on rotating shifts, the parent with a newborn, the student in exam week. Checked live, one copy, price card untouched. Then I did the thing I should have done first, and it is the reason this post exists. The page I fixed was not the page that receives the readers Every article I write links to my free-offer page, /free/ , not to the homepage.

articles.title: Stunning solar eclipse photos reveal giant hole and mysterious 'smoke rings' in the sun's atmosphere
articles.excerpt: Solar eclipse photography provides a unique vista into the processes taking place in the sun's upper atmosphere.
articles.body: Newly released photographs of the sun captured during the Aug. 12 total solar eclipse reveal the sun's outer atmosphere in unprecedented detail. The images, released by researchers working as part of the Solar Wind Sherpas project coordinated by the University of Hawaii, also show rare structures in the solar wind known as smoke rings. Named for their resemblance to the circles blown by smokers, these vortices were first identified in solar eclipse photographs captured in 2008. The researchers had long struggled to explain the processes behind their formation. They now know the rings are a result of the temperature differences in the coronal plasma and spread along the sun 's magnetic lines deep into interplanetary space.

articles.title: We urgently need to monitor AI agents’ actions in real time
articles.excerpt: This summer, hundreds of OpenAI agents tried to cheat on a cybersecurity test. They broke out of their test environment and successfully hacked Hugging Face, a site that they believed held clues about…
articles.body: This summer, hundreds of OpenAI agents tried to cheat on a cybersecurity test. They broke out of their test environment and successfully hacked Hugging Face, a site that they believed held clues about how they’d be graded. Around the same time, another OpenAI agent accessed private files from an Australian government website. It’s a problem that’s by no means confined to OpenAI. In the months since, Anthropic, Google, and Meta have also disclosed incidents in which their agents have gone off track. And worryingly, in many cases the agents eluded the very researchers and safety teams tasked with monitoring them.  AI agents are taking unauthorized actions, and the companies building and running them are mostly relying on luck and hindsight to mitigate any harmful impacts.

articles.title: SpaceX's Starfall capsule delivers cargo for US Air Force in landmark 'point to point' space mission
articles.excerpt: The U.S. Air Force has recovered experimental cargo launched aboard SpaceX's mysterious Starfall capsule, marking a step forward in the effort to assess the viability of rapid, point-to-point deliveri…
articles.body: The U.S. Air Force is opening up about the SpaceX Starfall cargo capsule it flew on a recent rideshare mission to orbit — and showing off what the capsule carried. The Air Force Research Laboratory (AFRL) completed a point-to-point rocket cargo delivery test using the secretive uncrewed reentry vehicle, confirming on social media its recovery of the package in the Pacific Ocean. "With support from SpaceX , the AFRL agile cargo pods were recovered after splashdown," the AFRL wrote in an X post on Oct. 26. The Starfall capsule launched on a Falcon 9 rocket as a part of SpaceX's Bandwagon-5 mission, which lifted off from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station on Oct. 20 .

articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 28, 1971: Britain launches its 1st satellite Prospero into space on a Black Arrow rocket
articles.excerpt: On Oct. 28, 1971, the United Kingdom launched its first satellite. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Oct. 28, 1971, the United Kingdom launched its first satellite. The satellite was named Prospero, but it was also known as the X-3. This wasn't Britain's first satellite , but it was the first and only one the British space program launched with one of its own rockets. The first six British satellites all launched from the United States on NASA rockets. Prospero launched on a carrier rocket called the Black Arrow. The Prospero mission was the fourth and final flight of a Black Arrow rocket . Prospero was designed to study how the environment in space affects communications satellites. It tested things solar cells and telemetry systems, and even had a micrometeoroid detector that would determine small particles in space posed a threat to the spacecraft.

articles.title: 5 days beneath the waves: What it's like to live in an underwater 'space station'
articles.excerpt: Confined inside a research station 22 feet (7 meters) underwater, Analog Astronaut Commander Dr. Musilova and her crew performed research and maintenance activities like future astronauts on Mars.
articles.body: Living underwater was surprisingly peaceful. It was in many ways exactly what I imagine living on Mars would be like one day. There were no humans around us, except for my three SEA STAR crewmembers and me. Apart from the human noises we made, we couldn't hear anything other than the life support systems keeping us alive submerged 22 feet (7 meters) below the surface. We were living in these extreme conditions to study the challenges astronauts may face on long-duration space missions. Since performing research in space is still rare and expensive, there are numerous facilities around the world that focus on recreating space-like conditions on Earth . One of those stations is the Jules' Undersea Lab, where the SEA STAR simulated space mission took place.
